chunks: "Plain UART connects exactly two devices, point to point. Each wire has a single driver: my TX drives your RX, and your TX drives my RX.
So the direction of communication is both ways at the same time, which is full duplex. There's no need to take turns, and no arbitration.
That's a strength for simplicity, but it's also the limitation.
If I want a third device, I can't just tie its TX onto the same wire, because two push-pull drivers on one line fight each other when one drives high and the other low.
There are standard ways around that. One, use more UARTs: one per device.

Two, use RS-485: a differential bus with tri-state drivers where up to 32 standard loads, or more with low-load transceivers, share a pair, and a protocol such as Modbus RTU says who talks when, so it becomes half duplex with addressing.
Three, some UARTs have a 9-bit mode where the ninth bit flags an address byte, so each device wakes up only when addressed.
Or four, if I need lots of devices, I'd choose I2C or SPI instead."
